To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
‘The haplotypic association between SNP haplotypes and a microsatellite in two human populations suggests that LD might be conserved over a large physical distance in non-Africans.’

(1) the SNP haplotypic diversity of the NOS-2 promoter region in Gambians is similar to that in Caucasians, but that (2) the haplotypic association with a highly polymorphic microsatellite is not conserved in either population, suggesting a high mutation rate of this microsatellite, and/or that the NOS2 promoter region has been a site of frequent recombination.

1) there is a dramatic loss of LD across a very short genetic distance in both Gambian and UK Caucasian populations, and 2) this suggests that the NOS2a-2.6 microsattelite has a high intrinsic mutation, or the SNP haplotyptypes are relatively ancient.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the genetic architecture of the human NOS2A gene, which is of interest because of its role in inflammation and its association with complex diseases, and with the genetic basis of LD between SNP markers and highly polymorphic microsatellite markers.
the development of genetic markers for association mapping and the investigation of the genetic basis of disease susceptibility.
the development of a new approach to the analysis of LD in human populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NOS2a−2.6 kb promoter region is highly variable in both populations studied, with a high proportion of the sequence variation residing in interspersed repetitive elements.
there is no LD between SNPs and the microsatellite at the NOS1A locus.
the haplotypic diversity in this region is maintained by recombination, and that the microsatellite is highly unstable, but not in an allele-specific manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the NOS2 locus is a good candidate locus for association studies in both populations, and that the NOS−2.6 pentanucleotide repeat should not be used as a marker in this region, as it is likely to be highly polymorphic and may be unstable in the laboratory.

LD is maintained over considerable genetic distances in non-African, and perhaps African populations, and that this is due to the ancient origin of haplotypes and/or the presence of interspersed repeats, rather than a high mutation rate of the microsatellite marker itself.
the haplotypic LD structure of the NOS-2A promoter is maintained over considerable genetic distances in non-African but not African populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LD can be maintained across a short genetic distance, even in non-African population.
the NOS2 microsatellite is not a good marker for association studies, and that the haplotype structure of the NOS 2A locus in Africans and Caucasians is more similar than previously reported.
LD is maintained over considerable genetic distances, supporting the use and interpretation of mixed marker haplotypes in association studies.
